questions.stem: In Domain-Driven Design, what does the term domain refer to?
options: The internet address of the company
The physical database schema
The network the servers run on
The problem area the business is working in, such as banking, healthcare, education or retail
The department that owns the data
questions.explanation: The domain is the problem area the business works in, for example banking, healthcare, education or retail.

questions.stem: What is the main goal of DDD Modelling?
options: To minimise storage costs
To standardise process diagram symbols
To normalise all tables to third normal form
To ensure system design closely reflects real business needs rather than technical convenience
To automate loan disbursement
questions.explanation: DDD encourages teams to model software around how the business actually operates so the system grows naturally alongside the business.

questions.stem: What is a ubiquitous language in DDD?
options: A programming language used by all developers
A universal metadata standard
A visual notation for processes
A query language for graph databases
The same terms used consistently by business experts, analysts and developers
questions.explanation: A shared or ubiquitous language means the same terms are used consistently by business experts, analysts and developers, reducing misunderstandings.

questions.stem: What is a bounded context in DDD?
options: A clearly defined area of the business where specific terms, rules and meanings apply consistently
A limit on the number of tables in a database
A security boundary around a server
A time limit on a process
A fixed list of allowed column values
questions.explanation: A bounded context is a clearly defined area of the business within which definitions are precise and agreed upon.

questions.stem: How does DDD handle the fact that large organisations use the same words differently in different parts of the business?
options: It forces one definition to fit everywhere
It bans the reuse of any term
It stores every meaning in a single glossary entry
It leaves the ambiguity unresolved
It accepts the reality and manages it by clearly separating contexts
questions.explanation: DDD accepts that words vary across the business and manages this by separating bounded contexts, each with its own clear meaning.

questions.stem: In the school example of bounded contexts, how might the same person be referred to in an alumni management context?
options: Applicant
Teacher
Former student
Guardian
Enrolled student
questions.explanation: In one context the person is a student currently enrolled; in alumni management the same person is a former student, treated as a separate context.

questions.stem: In the loan business example of DDD, which bounded context defines approval rules, thresholds and risk categories?
options: Credit Scoring context
Disbursement context
Risk Management context
Collections context
Customer context
questions.explanation: The Risk Management context defines approval rules, thresholds and risk categories; Credit Scoring covers score calculation and Disbursement covers payment and accounting.

questions.stem: How does DDD Modelling benefit analytics and reporting?
options: By storing reports inside the operational database
By ensuring analytical systems use the same domain definitions as operational systems, so metrics are calculated with consistent rules
By eliminating the need for metrics
By replacing dashboards with process diagrams
By merging all bounded contexts into one
questions.explanation: Analytical systems reuse the same domain definitions, so metrics like approval rates and default percentages are calculated consistently.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the nature of DDD Modelling?
options: It is business-driven but applied in technical system design, focusing on concepts, rules and language rather than tables or files
It is purely technical and focuses on physical tables
It is a visual notation defined by an international body
It focuses only on high-level roles and responsibilities
It is concerned mainly with raw data files
questions.explanation: DDD is business-driven but applied in technical design; it focuses on concepts, business rules and language consistency, not raw data structures.

questions.stem: In the comparison of Business Modelling, Process Modelling and DDD, which summary line is correct?
options: Business Modelling = how work flows; Process Modelling = who does what; DDD = shared language and contexts
Business Modelling = who does what; Process Modelling = how work flows; DDD = how to align systems with business contexts and language
Business Modelling = shared language; Process Modelling = who does what; DDD = how work flows
All three describe how work flows step by step
DDD = who does what; Business Modelling = how work flows; Process Modelling = bounded contexts
questions.explanation: The comparison shows the progression: Business Modelling is who does what, Process Modelling is how work flows, and DDD aligns systems with business contexts and language.
